article.title: History Becomes Expendable
article.author: Jason Steinhauer
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. What do Alaska, Wyoming, South Dakota and Vermont have in common? If you answered that none of these states offers a Ph.D. in History at any of its colleges or universities, you would be correct. I came across this fact while reading an article about the next state that might join the list: Oregon. According to a recent article in the Eugene-Springfield Lookout , the University of Oregon’s History Ph.D. program—which has existed since 1899—is being considered for elimination as the university seeks to bridge a $65 million budget deficit. While the University of Oregon athletics department generated more than $119 million last year, the school’s Education & General Fund projected a multi-million-dollar deficit. The university president explained in a recent email that tuition revenues accounted for 80 percent of that fund, most of it being out-of-state tuition (i.e., students and families who pay at- or close-to full price). As those enrollments have plummeted, the budget deficit has gotten wider. This necessitated a “different path,” to quote the president, elevating programs that “meet the needs” of industry and turning University of Oregon into a “destination of choice” for more students. It is likely that a History Ph.D. program does not satisfy either requirement: industry is not demanding more History Ph.D.’s, and a stellar doctorate program does not attract students as much as a winning College Football team. The University of Oregon is not unique; what is happening in Eugene, OR, is unfolding across the United States. Syracuse University in upstate New York is also facing a budget deficit after missing its enrollment targets. The Syracuse chancellor said in response that the school must “commit to differentiated academic excellence,” as it eliminated 93 academic programs . History was not one of them, but its Bachelor degrees in Citizenship and Civic Engagement, Classical Civilization, Digital Humanities, and History of Architecture were. Savannah State University, a Historically-Black College in Georgia, responded to declining enrollments and an $11 million budget gap by eliminating its History program. In 2023, Simmons College in Massachusetts cut several liberal arts majors in response to budget pressures, including History—and then in 2026, eliminated its Humanities major in the face of declining student revenue, outstanding loans and a downgrade of its credit rating. In Indiana, a bill passed last year to eliminate or consolidate over 400 programs at state universities, including in History, American Studies, Africana Studies and Political Science. And History has been on the chopping block at Montclair State University (New Jersey), University of Pittsburgh (Pennsylvania) and Missouri Western State University. Related: What Happened with Europe's Elections? Several converging trends are contributing. Fewer students have been enrolling in American colleges and universities over the past 15 years—though there has been a slight uptick since the Covid-19 pandemic. Smaller private universities have felt the decline the most, so much so that an estimated 150 private, nonprofit colleges have closed in the U.S. With fewer students now in high school due to declining birth rates—and more of those students signaling an interest in trade schools, community colleges or opting-out of higher education altogether—experts expect a continued decline in student tuition dollars through the 2030s, which will lead to more program cuts and campus closures. American colleges and universities have also experienced a decline in international students. International students dropped during the Covid-19 pandemic, rose in subsequent years, then took a steep downturn since 2025. Since international students often pay full price tuition (as opposed to American students who receive financial aid and scholarships), the losses have an outsized influence. Amid the decline in students overall, there have also been cultural forces altering student priorities and interests. The past 20 years have seen a heavy emphasis on science, technology, engineering and math (S.T.E.M.) in the private, public and nonprofit sectors, which has drawn student and parents towards S.T.E.M. and A.I. degrees and away from Liberal Arts and Humanities degrees. In recent years, a nationwide shortage of nurses and doctors have also led to boons for medical and nursing schools, with baccalaureate and higher degree nursing programs seeing increased enrollments across the board . The same cannot be said for History programs. According to the most recent data , between 2012 and 2025, the number of History degrees declined more than 40 percent in the U.S. Dissertations in the field declined by nearly 50 percent. In the humanities more broadly—to include subjects such as Religion, Philosophy, English and others—degrees awarded at American universities were the lowest since 1991. The ratio of humanities degrees to overall degrees in the U.S. is now at the lowest level since comprehensive data became available. Robert Townsend—who I knew when he worked at the American Historical Association and I worked at the Library of Congress—has been monitoring these trends for years in his current role at the American Academy of Arts & Sciences. When the most recent figures were released, he was quoted in several media outlets about the root causes. In his view, critical factors included students’ declining comfort with long-form reading, and their difficulty envisioning what they would do with a humanities degree after college. In other words, because young people read far less than they once did, and reading scores among high school seniors are at their lowest levels in 30 years , the hefty history books required by college-level courses feel like an insurmountable burden for incoming undergraduates. While engaging with such books might answer student questions about the past, it does not help them answer their questions about the future: their future careers, their future job prospects or their future contributions to society. To put it another way, student anxieties about the future are inhibiting them from learning about the past. Townsend also added that the cost of college compels students (and parents) to choose majors with a clearer career path and an attractive starting salary. Different sources have varying statistics, but on the aggregate the cost of higher education in the U.S. has significantly outpaced the rate of inflation, with tuition increasing nearly 15 percent over the past 20 years when adjusted for inflation, and nearly 84 percent when not. Despite scholarships, financial assistance, and new efforts to reduce costs, a college education in the U.S. is still exorbitantly expensive, more so for private colleges than public universities or community colleges. At such prices, students and parents opt for majors they perceive to have more certain career trajectories. Finally, as I wrote in my book History, Disrupted , it is also the case that billions of pieces of “ e -history ” now exist online for free. From Wikipedia to YouTube, podcasts to TikTok videos, one could consume historical content on the social Web from now until the end of time and never reach the end. Without re-litigating the argument on whether such content is “good” or “bad” ( read the book to answer that question), it is unmistakably the case that students do not need to pay $37,000 in tuition each year to get exposed to information about the past. The over-abundance of “free” history online complicates the argument for why students and parents should pay for formal history instruction in school, especially if they do not plan to pursue a career in the field. Regardless of which factors are most prevailing, History is declining within American higher ed—and, indeed, even in high schools and middle schools. And while it may be tempting to assign responsibility to political factors, the reality is that the decline has unfolded over a 20-year period during both parties’ leadership at the federal, state and local levels. Elected officials and school administrators have been unable to do much to alter these trajectories, which show no signs of abating. What could realistically be done? Should something be done? As a reader of this newsletter, you might agree the answer to the second question is ‘yes.’ But not everyone feels similarly. Perhaps this is merely the “market” at work, some people have argued. If there is no demand for History degrees at the collegiate level, then supply diminishes. If there are no students enrolling in History courses, it becomes difficult to justify funding them. If there are no jobs for History majors, then students cannot be faulted for pursuing other options. The answer, it seems, would be to either stimulate more demand among employers, students and parents for History degrees, likely by making History courses more attractive to young people, less predicated on reading and writing, and connecting them directly to other areas of the workforce (e.g., History of Nursing or History of A.I.); or insist that History education is so essential that it be required regardless of student interest, with the requisite funding coming from governments, donations or endowments. In my final chapter of History, Disrupted , titled “ Does History Have a Future ?” I did proffer one potential solution: remove History from the undergraduate curriculum under the stipulation that students must return later in life to complete the coursework. My thinking was that until college becomes significantly less expensive, students will continue to pursue degrees with higher earning capacity in the shortest amount of time. During those anxious early adult years, History courses may not be the best investment of their time and money. But as older adults, hopefully with steady income and a career underway, as well as being more attuned to the realities of contributing to a healthy democracy, History courses will be more relevant to them. Such an approach may not be viable in practice, but a wicked problem such as this probably will require some outside-the-box thinking to solve. In closing, though, I will deviate from solutions to a wider view on what this reality portends for us. Our young people already know so little about history; this surely means they will know less. Our young people already read so little and so infrequently; this means they will do so less. They are already susceptible to historical propaganda and disinformation, and this means they will be more so. And they will enter the wider world with little connection to the world that was made before they arrived in it, with no deep understanding of the fields, professions and forces that are shaping their lives. It is not the case that a decline in History education solely dictates these realities; there are many factors. But the decline in History education contributes to them, and in many ways is emblematic of the broader challenges we face. We are increasingly illiterate, increasingly fixated on “costs” as opposed to “value,” and increasingly privileging our proverbial left-brain at the expense of our right. With an election coming up, it is worth pausing to consider how historically illiterate our electorate is becoming, and what that means for our democracy. Reading and thinking about the past does, indeed, affect the future. History may not move the bottom line as much as TV sports contracts or grants from tech companies. But if colleges and universities are solely worried about the “bottom” line, then we may as well stop calling them “higher” education. Cutting and cutting until we reach the “bottom” may tidy up the spreadsheet, but it does little to enrich the lives, minds and “higher” faculties of young people. That mission remains worthy of our investment, whatever the costs.
